title: Dimensional Crossover of Mass Anisotropy in Ta-doped WTe2
authors: P. Das, D. Das, P. Kumar, Monika, S. Patnaik
abstract: The observation of extremely large magnetoresistance in WTe2 has attracted considerable attention towards understanding its underlying origin. With its layered van der Waals structure, the question that remains largely unexplored is whether the three-dimensional anisotropic transport characteristics of WTe2 persists under chemical substitution. Here, we present a systematic angle-dependent magneto-transport study of single-crystalline TaxW1-xTe2 (x = 0, 0.05, 0.1). The results are analysed within a mass anisotropy scaling framework to extract the mass anisotropy parameter γ as a function of temperature and doping. It is observed that Ta substitution leads to monotonic increase of γ across all temperatures, indicating a progressive deepening of quasi-two-dimensional Fermi surface character. Ta doping also leads to a substantial improvement in crystalline quality, reflected in a pronounced increase in the residual resistivity ratio. Despite weakening electron-hole compensation, the magnetoresistance rises sharply to ~58,211% at x = 0.1, which is assigned to a substantial enhancement in carrier mobility. Rietveld refinement confirms a systematic c-axis contraction with Ta content, identifying the structural origin of the enhanced anisotropy. The mass anisotropy scaling that holds for x = 0 and x = 0.05 breaks down for x = 0.1, where the angular magneto-resistance anisotropy substantially exceeds single-ellipsoid predictions, pointing to a multi-pocket Fermi surface with distinct anisotropies. Nonlinear Hall resistivity provides independent evidence for the underlying multiband character of transport in this system. These findings demonstrate that Fermi surface anisotropy, carrier compensation, and mobility are independent parameters that can lead to tuneable control of large magnetoresistance in topological semimetal WTe2.
summary: This work systematically studies Ta-doping in WTe2, demonstrating that doping enhances carrier mobility and deepens 2D character, leading to record magnetoresistance. The study reveals that while anisotropy is tunable, the system undergoes a transition to a multi-pocket Fermi surface at higher doping levels. Overall, it establishes that key transport parameters—anisotropy, compensation, and mobility—can be independently controlled in this topological semimetal.
main_problem: The study investigates whether the anisotropic transport characteristics of WTe2 persist when chemically substituted with Ta, and how doping affects the control mechanisms behind large magnetoresistance (XMR).
main_result: Ta substitution enhances carrier mobility and deepens quasi-two-dimensional Fermi surface character, leading to record high MR values; however, at higher doping levels, the system transitions to a multi-pocket Fermi surface regime.
method: The research combines angle-dependent magnetotransport measurements with structural analysis (XRD) and fitting data using mass anisotropy scaling frameworks.
model_or_system: The physical system is single-crystalline Ta-doped WTe2 ($	ext{Ta}_x	ext{W}_{1-x}	ext{Te}_2$), a layered van der Waals semimetal. Analysis employs semiclassical models for magnetoresistance and nonlinear Hall resistivity to probe multiband transport.
key_observables: Magnetoresistance (MR) up to 58,211%; mass anisotropy parameter ($\gamma$); effective carrier mobility ($\mu_{	ext{eff}}$); residual resistivity ratio (RRR).
important_parameters: Doping concentration ($x=0, 0.05, 0.1$); Temperature ($T$); Magnetic field strength ($B$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the mass anisotropy scaling framework and semiclassical models for transport phenomena.
figures_summary: Figures show XRD patterns confirming $c$-axis contraction with Ta content, and magnetotransport curves demonstrating a sharp rise in MR at $x=0.1$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the effect of Ta doping on crystal structure (XRD), transport anisotropy ($\gamma$ scaling), carrier dynamics ($\mu_{	ext{eff}}$ enhancement), and Fermi surface topology (breakdown of single-ellipsoid scaling, nonlinear Hall response).
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter physics, the ability to tune electronic properties (anisotropy, mobility) via chemical doping provides a model for engineering quantum states or transport channels relevant to advanced quantum devices.

All compositions show metallic behaviour. Figure 4. Effective carrier mobility μeff as a function of temperature for single-crystalline TaxW1-xTe2 (x = 0, 0.05, 0.1) at 5 K, 30 K, and 50 K. At 5 K, the mobility of Ta0.1W0.9Te2 (~65 × 10⁴ cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹) is more than double that of pristine WTe2 (~31 × 10⁴ cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹), consistent with the dramatically enhanced MR at x = 0.1.

Figure 3. Transverse magnetoresistance MR(%) as a function of magnetic field B at 5 K for single- crystalline TaxW1-xTe2 (x = 0, 0.05, 0.1), with H applied along the c axis. All compositions display large, non-saturating parabolic MR up to 5 T. The MR evolves non-monotonically with Ta content, decreasing from 22,379% (x = 0) to 15,537% (x = 0.05) before rising sharply to 58,211% (x = 0.1) at 5 T. The inset shows the measurement geometry, with current I flowing along the b axis and field H applied along the c axis.

Angle-dependent magnetoresistance of pristine WTe2 at (a) 5 K, (b) 30 K, and (c) 50 K for field orientations θ = 0°, 30°, 60°, and 90°, where θ is the angle between the applied field H and the crystallographic c axis.
